intro: Haarlemmermeer is a municipality built on a lake bed: engineers pumped the Haarlemmermeer dry between 1849 and 1852, and every tree here has grown on ground that did not exist as farmland before that. Its five registered trees spread across three villages inside the polder, Hoofddorp, Vijfhuizen and Badhoevedorp: a wingnut saved from a shopping centre, a lime planted for a royal jubilee, a plane that predates the street around it.
meta_description: Five registered trees across the Haarlemmermeer polder, all planted since the lake was drained in 1852: a wingnut, a jubilee lime, a plane and more.
question_meta: Haarlemmermeer's oldest tree is a London plane from the 1880s in Hoofddorp, older than the notary's office it now fronts. Here it is, and four more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Haarlemmermeer is the London Plane of Hoofddorp, registered to a planting around 1885, roughly 140 years old. It grows on municipal ground at the corner of the Hoofdweg and the Manegelaan, in front of a notary's office, predating both the office and most of the street around it.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every figure on this page is a band. The register is the single source for all five trees, so every entry ships flagged rather than confirmed. Three stand in Hoofddorp; the other two are in Vijfhuizen and Badhoevedorp, villages within the same municipality rather than one walkable city. All of them grow on ground that was open water until three steam pumping engines drained the Haarlemmermeer between 1849 and 1852, which is why nothing here predates the mid nineteenth century: the whole polder is younger than most Dutch town centres. One tree, a roadside maple in Badhoevedorp, stands on private land and can only be seen from the street, never approached, and the register says so plainly. Where a pin is marked approximate, we know the site and not the exact trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Haarlemmermeer?
faq.a: The London Plane of Hoofddorp, registered to a planting around 1885. It grows on municipal ground at the corner of the Hoofdweg and the Manegelaan, in front of a notary's office, and the register credits it for its remarkable form as much as its age.

faq.q: Why is the ground in Haarlemmermeer so young for old trees?
faq.a: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, most of this municipality was the Haarlemmermeer itself, a lake wide enough to frighten Amsterdam. Three steam pumping engines drained it between 1849 and 1852, and everything planted here since then, including every tree on this page, is younger than the drainage.

faq.q: Can I visit all five of these trees on one walk?
faq.a: Not quite. Three are in Hoofddorp; the others are in Vijfhuizen and Badhoevedorp, several kilometres away. Each village is its own short stop rather than part of one route.

faq.q: Can I walk up to the maple on the Nieuwemeerdijk?
faq.a: No. It grows in the front garden of a private house that is still lived in. It is clearly visible from the road the whole way past, which is why it made this list, but there is no gate to try and no reason to open one.

trees.name: The Wingnut of the Hoofddorp Market
trees.age_estimate: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1935

location.address: Markt, in front of the market hall, Hoofddorp

trees.story:
When Hoofddorp built a new shopping centre around its market square, the municipality made saving this tree a condition of the plan. That is on the record as the reason it is still there, planted, the register says, around 1935, in front of what is now the market hall.

Caucasian wingnut is not a tree many Dutch town squares grow. It comes from wet valley floors in the Caucasus and northern Iran, suckers readily from its own roots, and in midsummer it hangs strings of winged nutlets half a metre long from every branch tip, for a few weeks looking like a tree decked out for a parade nobody announced.

Being kept during redevelopment is not the same as being cared for since, and the register does not say anything about its condition today. What it records is a species and a rough decade, and nothing else has been published about this particular tree.

It stands in the middle of Hoofddorp, free to walk up to any day of the week. If you know more about why the council insisted on keeping it, tell us.

best_time.label: midsummer, when strings of winged nutlets half a metre long hang from every branch

trees.access: Free, on the Markt in front of the market hall, always visible.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in midsummer by strings of winged nutlets hanging half a metre long from every branch tip. It stands on the Markt, in front of the market hall, Hoofddorp.

trees.name: The Jubilee Lime of Vijfhuizen
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 years, from a registered planting date around 1910
trees.story:
In 1923 the Netherlands marked twenty five years of Queen Wilhelmina on the throne, and this lime went into the ground in Vijfhuizen to mark it, one of many jubilee trees planted across the country that year. The register keeps the reason on file even though almost nothing else about the tree has been written down.

It stands on the Spieringweg opposite a spot known locally as the Fortwachter, in what the register calls a plantsoen: an ordinary municipal planting strip rather than a park. A common lime grown out in the open like this builds a dense, rounded crown down to head height, and in July it does what limes do everywhere: small pale flowers open in hanging clusters, the tree hums with bees for a couple of weeks, and the scent carries across the road.

A century is not old for a lime, which can run to several, but it is old for anything standing in the Haarlemmermeer, ground that was still open water until 1852. The register is the only source that has looked at this specific tree. If you know more about the planting or the jubilee it marked, tell us.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the scent carries across the Spieringweg

trees.access: Free, alongside a public road, always visible.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dense, rounded crown reaching down to head height, standing in an ordinary planting strip. It stands on the Spieringweg, opposite the Fortwachter, Vijfhuizen.

trees.name: The London Plane of Hoofddorp
trees.age_estimate: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1885
trees.story:
Locals use this plane tree to navigate by. The register's whole reasoning for designating it monumental is two words: remarkable form, landmark, and that is the sum of what has been written about it.

It grows on municipal ground in front of a notary's office at the corner of the Hoofdweg and the Manegelaan, planted, the register estimates, somewhere in the 1880s, which would make it Hoofddorp's oldest registered tree by a wide margin over almost everything else on this page. London plane is a hybrid that barely exists in the wild, first bred in seventeenth century Europe by crossing an American and an Oriental species, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, pollution and hard pruning better than almost anything else available, which is why it lines so many European streets and squares. Its bark flakes away in patches instead of splitting, so the trunk carries a camouflage pattern of grey, green and cream that keeps changing as old plates drop off.

At around 140 years old it predates the notary's office, the Manegelaan and most of what stands near it now. The register is the only source that has looked at it. If you know when it actually went in, tell us.
trees.access: Free, on municipal ground in front of a notary's office, visible from the Hoofdweg.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its bark flaking away in a camouflage pattern of grey, green and cream. It stands in front of a notary's office at Hoofdweg 669, corner of Manegelaan.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Ring Road
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 years, from a registered planting date around 1910

location.address: Hoofdweg, corner of the Rijksweg ring road, Hoofddorp

trees.story:
The register's own 2024 inspection ends on an unusually candid note: the tree, it says, is not doing well these days. That is close to an editorial opinion for a database this dry.

The weeping beech stands with a handful of ordinary beeches on a corner where the Hoofdvaart, the canal cut straight through the drained lake to the old pumping station, meets the ring road that now circles Hoofddorp. The register's own guess is that before the ring road existed, this corner might have been a small park; if so, the road took most of it, and what is left reads as a traffic island with trees on it rather than the parkland setting the tree wants. Planted, the register estimates, between 1900 and 1910, it is around a century old.

A weeping beech is not a natural form. Every one alive descends by graft or cutting from a single tree found wild in Germany around 1680, propagated ever since because its branches fall instead of rising, so a mature specimen makes a tent of foliage with the trunk hidden somewhere inside. Squeezed onto a traffic corner and hemmed in by road, this one has never had the room to do that properly, which may be exactly what the register means.

The register is the only source. If you know this tree, tell us how it is doing now.
trees.access: Free, on a public road corner, always visible.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its falling branches forming a tent shape, hemmed onto a traffic island rather than open parkland. It stands where the Hoofdweg meets the ring road, Hoofddorp.

trees.name: The Roadside Maple of Badhoevedorp
trees.age_estimate: roughly 110 years, from a registered planting date around 1915, though the register's own note suggests 1895
trees.story:
This maple stands in the front garden of a house on the Nieuwemeerdijk built in 1915, and the register cannot quite agree with itself about which of the two is older. Its structured record bands the planting to 1910-1920. Its own descriptive note gives 1895 instead, and adds that if that figure is right, the tree was already growing on this dike before the house went up beside it. Both cannot be true, and we have not been able to resolve which the register meant.

The register names it a sycamore, Acer pseudoplatanus, which the Dutch call the gewone esdoorn.

None of the uncertainty affects what a passerby can see: a full, healthy crown that the register itself calls the single most striking thing about this stretch of the Nieuwemeerdijk, visible the whole way along the road. The tree grows in the garden of a house that is still lived in, so this is a look rather than a visit. There is no gate to try and no reason to open one, just a wide view from the roadside.

The register is the only source that has looked at this tree, and on its own evidence it has not entirely made up its mind.
trees.access: Visible from the Nieuwemeerdijk; the tree grows in a private front garden and cannot be approached.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its full, healthy crown, visible the whole way along the road from a private front garden. It stands at Nieuwemeerdijk 143, Badhoevedorp.
